summary: Defines the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules, giving common data types such as shared formats a name. It is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 1903.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP management data is written in MIB modules, and those modules often need data types that are more specific than the basic ones, such as a hardware address or a yes-or-no flag. RFC 2579 defines a way to name such types and gives a shared starting set that every MIB module can use.

questions: what is a textual convention in snmp
how are snmp table rows created
subtitle: A way to give MIB data types their own names, meanings and display formats, plus the first set of ready-made ones.

tldr.problem: MIB designers often need types that are like the SMI base types but with a different name and more precise meaning, such as a MAC address or a boolean.
tldr.mechanism: The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro names a new type, gives its syntax, status, description and an optional display hint, and the RFC defines an initial set including DisplayString, MacAddress, TruthValue, RowStatus, TimeStamp and DateAndTime.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 58) that obsoletes RFC 1903. Objects using a textual convention are still encoded by the rules of their underlying primitive type.

today: RFC 2579 is an Internet Standard (STD 58) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1903 and is the textual-conventions companion to RFC 2578 in the SMIv2 family.

sections.title: Why Textual Conventions Exist
sections.content:
MIB modules are written in the adapted ASN.1 subset called the Structure of Management Information. The first version, SMIv1, is described in RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215; the current version is SMIv2, defined in RFC 2578.

When designing a module it is often useful to define new types similar to the SMI types: a different name, a similar syntax, but more precise semantics. These are textual conventions, used for the convenience of humans reading the MIB module. Objects defined with a textual convention are always encoded by the rules of their primitive type, so nothing changes on the wire.

The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro conveys the syntax and semantics of such a type. Its expansion conceptually happens at implementation time, not at run time. This document defines the initial set of textual conventions available to all MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: A textual convention is a nickname for a specific kind of value, with a written meaning attached. It makes MIB modules easier for people to read, and it does not change how the value is sent over the network.

sections.title: The TEXTUAL-CONVENTION Macro
sections.content:
The macro has an optional DISPLAY-HINT clause, a required STATUS clause (with the values current, deprecated or obsolete), a required DESCRIPTION clause, an optional REFERENCE clause and a required SYNTAX clause. The syntax must be a base type or the BITS construct, so the SYNTAX clause of a textual convention cannot refer to a previously defined textual convention.

A convention's name must consist of letters and digits with an upper-case initial character. It must not conflict with the reserved words of RFC 2578, should not be all upper case, and must not exceed 64 characters; names longer than 32 characters are not recommended. The hyphen is not allowed, except in information modules converted from SMIv1, and names used in all standard information modules must be unique.

The SYNTAX clause may be sub-typed in the same way as the SYNTAX clause of an OBJECT-TYPE macro. Size, range or enumeration restrictions represent the maximal level of support that makes protocol sense.

The STATUS clause marks whether the definition is current or historic: current means valid; obsolete means it should not be implemented; deprecated also indicates an obsolete definition but permits new or continued implementation to foster interoperability with older implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: To define a new label you give it a name, a status, a written meaning and the kind of value it holds underneath. The name rules keep labels unique and readable across all standard MIB modules.

sections.title: The Initial Set of Conventions
sections.content:
Text and addresses. DisplayString is NVT ASCII text (character codes 0-127, with the special meanings defined in RFC 854), at most 255 characters, with display hint 255a. PhysAddress is a media- or physical-level address, and MacAddress is an 802 MAC address of exactly 6 octets in the canonical order of IEEE 802.1a. TDomain denotes a kind of transport service, and TAddress is a transport address of 1 to 255 octets that is always read in the context of a TDomain.

Values and identifiers. TruthValue is an integer with true(1) and false(2). TestAndIncr supports atomic operations: a set succeeds only if the supplied value exactly matches the current one, and then the value is incremented, wrapping to zero after 2147483647. AutonomousType is an independently extensible type identification OBJECT IDENTIFIER. VariablePointer points to a specific object instance such as sysContact.0, and RowPointer points to a conceptual row. The older InstancePointer is marked obsolete and replaced by those two.

Time and storage. TimeStamp holds the value of sysUpTime when something happened; the text notes that after approximately 497 days without re-initialization sysUpTime wraps around, which can leave existing TimeStamp values ambiguous. TimeInterval is a period in units of 0.01 seconds. DateAndTime is an 8 or 11 octet value covering year, month, day, hour, minutes, seconds, deci-seconds and an optional offset from UTC. StorageType describes how a row is kept: other(1), volatile(2), nonVolatile(3), permanent(4) or readOnly(5).
sections.plainLanguage: The starter set has labels for text, hardware addresses, yes-or-no values, dates and times, counters for retries, pointers to other objects, and how long a row of information should be remembered.

sections.title: RowStatus: Creating and Deleting Rows
sections.content:
RowStatus manages the creation and deletion of conceptual rows, and is the syntax of a row's status column. It has six values. active(1) and notInService(2) may be read or written, notReady(3) may only be read, and createAndGo(4), createAndWait(5) and destroy(6) are actions that may be written but are never read. Reading a row's status therefore returns only notReady, notInService or active.

The RFC walks through four interactions for creating a row: selecting an instance-identifier that is not in use, creating the conceptual row, initializing columns for which the agent supplies no default, and making the row available. A station can create and activate in one set with createAndGo, which fails with inconsistentValue if the agent lacks enough information. Or it can use createAndWait, fill in the missing columns step by step, and finally set the status to active. An agent that does not support createAndWait answers wrongValue.

If a station never finishes, the row would sit in notInService or notReady forever, consuming resources. The agent must detect rows left that way for an abnormally long time and remove them. Unless the status column's DESCRIPTION clause says otherwise, the suggested period is approximately 5 minutes. Setting destroy deletes all instances of the row whatever its current state. Whenever any elements of a row exist, the RowStatus column must also exist.
sections.plainLanguage: RowStatus is how a management station creates and removes table rows. It can create and open a row in one step, or create it quietly, fill in the columns, and open it later. If a station starts a row and never finishes, the device removes the leftover row after a while.

sections.title: Display Hints
sections.content:
A DISPLAY-HINT clause suggests how to show a value. It must not be present when the convention is defined with a syntax of OBJECT IDENTIFIER, IpAddress, Counter32, Counter64 or any enumerated syntax (BITS or INTEGER).

For syntaxes with an underlying INTEGER, the hint is a format character: x for hexadecimal, d for decimal, o for octal or b for binary. For d it can be followed by a hyphen and a number giving the implied decimal point, so d-2 renders a value of 1234 as 12.34. Leading zeros are omitted when rendering.

For OCTET STRING syntaxes the hint is a list of octet-format specifications, each with five parts: an optional repeat indicator (an asterisk), an octet length, a display format (x, d, o, a for ASCII or t for UTF-8), an optional separator character and an optional repeat terminator. MacAddress uses 1x:, meaning each octet is shown in hexadecimal followed by a colon. Octets are processed most significant first, and if octets remain after the last specification, the last one is re-applied until none are left.
sections.plainLanguage: A display hint is a note saying how to print a value, such as putting a decimal point in the right place or writing a hardware address as pairs of hex digits with colons between them.

sections.title: Revising a Convention
sections.content:
A textual convention may be revised only if the change has no potential to cause interoperability problems over the wire between an implementation using the original specification and one using the updated specification. Anything else requires a new convention with a new name.

The allowed revisions are: adding enumerations or changing labels in an enumerated INTEGER or BITS construct; moving a STATUS value of current to deprecated or obsolete, or deprecated to obsolete, with an updated DESCRIPTION explaining the rationale; adding or updating a REFERENCE clause; adding or updating a DISPLAY-HINT clause; clarifying or extending the DESCRIPTION clause; and any editorial change.

Because the TEXTUAL-CONVENTION macro now exists, an older definition such as DisplayString ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE (0..255)) should be replaced by a TEXTUAL-CONVENTION when a module is revised.
sections.plainLanguage: You can fix the wording of a label or retire it, but if a change would alter how old and new devices interpret the value on the wire, you must invent a new label with a new name instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a means to define new data types for the language used to write and read descriptions of management information. It states that these data types have no security impact on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: These are only labels for writing management data down, so the RFC concludes that they add no security risk.

viz.caption: THE SIX ROWSTATUS VALUES FROM RFC 2579

items.label: active
items.desc: Row is available for use by the managed device. Readable and writable.

items.label: notInService
items.desc: Row exists but is unavailable. Readable and writable.

items.label: notReady
items.desc: Row exists but required information is missing. Read only.

items.label: createAndGo
items.desc: Create a row and make it active. Write only.

items.label: createAndWait
items.desc: Create a row without making it available. Write only.

items.label: destroy
items.desc: Delete all instances of the row. Write only.
